sky: eclipse
Assyrian eclipse of Bur-Sagale
Assyrian eponym lists record a solar eclipse in the year of Bur-Sagale, identified in 1867 with 15 June 763 BC. It anchors the absolute chronology of the ancient Near East.

Wikipedia (citing Rawlinson 1867)

Earliest aurora candidates in Assyrian tablets

Assyrian astrological reports from about 680-650 BCE describe a 'red glow' and 'red covers the sky', recorded at Nineveh and Babylon. They match an extreme solar particle event around 660 BCE seen in cosmogenic isotopes.

Eclipse of Thales halts the Medes and Lydians

Herodotus says day turned to night during a battle between the Medes and Lydians, who then made peace; Thales had foretold it. It is usually dated 28 May 585 BC; the Halys site is a scholarly assumption.
Eclipse of Thales
Herodotus via Wikipedia

Halley's Comet: first certain record, in China's Records of the Grand Historian
The first confirmed sighting of Halley's Comet, seen in May-June 240 BC after perihelion on 30 March. It is described in the Chinese Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian).
Halley's Comet

Seen from 26 August to 20 October 12 BC at about magnitude -5, passing 0.16 AU from Earth. Chinese astronomers watched it for two months.
Halley's Comet

A 'guest star' appears near Alpha Centauri; Han astronomers record it
The Book of Later Han records a guest star appearing on 7 December 185 that faded after about eight months. It is the oldest recorded supernova; its remnant is RCW 86.
SN 185

A guest star flares in Scorpius, recorded by Chinese astronomers
Chinese records note a guest star in the tail of Scorpius from about March to November 393, peaking near magnitude -1. It is a probable supernova, possibly remnant RX J1713.7-3946.
SN 393
Wikipedia (SN 393)

Miyake event: radiocarbon spike in Japanese cedars

Annual rings of Japanese cedars from Yaku Island show a rapid rise of about 12 per mil in carbon-14 from AD 774 to 775, about 20 times the normal solar change. It is now attributed to an extreme solar particle event.
774–775 carbon-14 spike
Miyake et al. 2012, Nature; National Geographic
comet
Halley's Comet makes its closest-ever approach to Earth
On 10 April 837 Halley's Comet passed about 0.033 AU from Earth, its closest known approach, reaching roughly magnitude -3 to -3.5. It was visible from 22 March to 28 April.
Halley's Comet
NASA; Wikipedia (Halley's Comet)
supernova
SN 1006, the brightest star in recorded history, blazes in Lupus
Seen from Egypt, China, Yemen and Switzerland from late April 1006, it reached about magnitude -7.5. Ali ibn Ridwan described it, and it stayed visible for well over a year.
Wikipedia (SN 1006); Songshi; Annales Sangallenses maiores
supernova
A supernova blazes in Taurus; Song astronomers record a 'guest star'
Recorded by Song-era Chinese astronomers from 4 July 1054, it was visible in daylight for 23 days and at night until April 1056. Its remnant is the Crab Nebula with its pulsar.
Wikipedia (SN 1054); Song Huiyao
comet
Halley's Comet appears before Hastings, later stitched into the Bayeux Tapestry
Visible from 3 April to 7 June 1066 at about magnitude -4, it was taken as an omen and is depicted in the Bayeux Tapestry showing the Battle of Hastings.
Halley's Comet
NASA; Wikipedia (Halley's Comet)
supernova
A guest star appears in Cassiopeia for six months
Chinese and Japanese astronomers recorded a new star in Cassiopeia from early August 1181 that stayed visible for 185 days. Pa 30 is now its leading candidate remnant.
Wikipedia (SN 1181)
comet

Seen from 1 September to 31 October 1301 at about magnitude -1. Giotto di Bondone painted it as the star in his Adoration of the Magi.
Halley's Comet
Wikipedia (Halley's Comet)

Halley's Comet
Wikipedia (Halley's Comet)
comet
Halley's Comet: Apian notes comet tails point away from the Sun
Seen from 1 August to 8 September 1531 at about magnitude -1. Petrus Apianus observed that the comet's tail always points away from the Sun.
Halley's Comet
Wikipedia (Halley's Comet)
supernova
Tycho Brahe's 'new star' in Cassiopeia shatters the unchanging heavens
Appearing in early November 1572, it peaked around magnitude -4 on 16 November and stayed visible to the naked eye into early 1574. Tycho described it in De nova stella (1573).
Wikipedia (SN 1572)
comet
Tycho Brahe proves the Great Comet lies beyond the Moon
First seen on 1 November 1577 and watched by Tycho from Hven from 13 November, at about magnitude -3. Comparing his measurements with Hajek's in Prague, he showed it lay far beyond the Moon.
Great Comet of 1577
Wikipedia (Great Comet of 1577)

Great aurora of March 1582, Japan to Portugal
A severe magnetic storm on 6-8 March 1582 produced aurorae recorded in East Asia and in Lisbon, Portugal. The lowest-latitude sighting was at Bungo, Japan (33.2 N).

Kepler's Supernova in Ophiuchus, the last seen in our galaxy
First recorded on 9 October 1604 and observed by Kepler in Prague from 17 October, it peaked near magnitude -2.5 and was visible to the naked eye for 18 months.
Kepler's Supernova
Wikipedia (Kepler's Supernova)
comet
Halley's Comet observed by Johannes Kepler
Seen from 21 September to 26 October 1607 at about magnitude 0 and observed by Johannes Kepler. Halley later linked the comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 as one returning object.
Halley's Comet
NASA; Wikipedia (Halley's Comet)
transit
Jeremiah Horrocks makes the first observation of a transit of Venus
On 4 December 1639 Horrocks at Much Hoole and William Crabtree at Broughton made the first recorded observation of a transit of Venus. Horrocks estimated the Sun's distance at 95.6 million km.
Jeremiah Horrocks
Wikipedia (Transit of Venus)

Kirch finds the Great Comet of 1680, the first discovered by telescope

Gottfried Kirch found it at Coburg on 14 November 1680, the first comet discovered by telescope. It grazed the Sun on 18 December, was reputedly visible by day, and Newton used it to test Kepler's laws.
Great Comet of 1680
Wikipedia (Great Comet of 1680)
comet
Edmond Halley watches the comet that will bear his name
Seen from 15 August to 21 September 1682 and observed by Edmond Halley at Islington. Using Newton's gravity he identified it with the comets of 1531 and 1607 and predicted its return.
Halley's Comet
NASA; Wikipedia (Halley's Comet)

Halley's eclipse over London
Edmond Halley predicted and mapped the path of totality; his forecast was off by about four minutes and 30 km. London saw 3 min 33 s of totality.

Wikipedia
comet
De Cheseaux's comet fans out six tails above the horizon
Discovered in late 1743, it may have reached magnitude -7 around perihelion on 1 March 1744. In early March de Cheseaux at Lausanne and others saw a fan of six tails rise above the horizon.
Great Comet of 1744
Wikipedia (Great Comet of 1744)

Halley's Comet

On 6 June 1761 Mason and Dixon observed from the Cape of Good Hope, and Lomonosov in St Petersburg inferred that Venus has an atmosphere. French expeditions went to Siberia, Madagascar and beyond.
Transit of Venus
Wikipedia (Transit of Venus)

Captain Cook observes the transit of Venus from Tahiti
On 3 June 1769 James Cook and Charles Green timed the transit at Point Venus, Tahiti, while Maximilian Hell observed from Vardo, Norway. Combined results put the Sun at about 151-153 million km.
1769 transit of Venus observed from Tahiti
Wikipedia (Transit of Venus)

A red aurora was painted and described over Kyoto on 17 September 1770, during nearly nine nights of low-latitude aurorae. Captain Cook's crew saw it near Timor at about 10.5 S; the storm may have rivalled the 1859 Carrington event.

Great Comet of 1811

On 12-13 November 1833 the Leonids peaked at over 100,000 meteors an hour across North America east of the Rockies. The storm launched serious meteor science.
Leonids

First photograph of a total solar eclipse
At Konigsberg's Royal Prussian Observatory, daguerreotypist Julius Berkowski made an 84-second exposure soon after totality began. It was the first scientifically useful photograph of the corona.

Found by Giovanni Donati at Florence on 2 June 1858, it reached about magnitude 0-1 and became a brilliant curved-tail sight in October. It was photographed on 27 September, the first comet photograph.

Carrington Event: the great solar storm of 1859

On 1 September 1859 Richard Carrington saw a white-light solar flare; about 17 hours later aurorae lit skies as far as Panama and telegraph systems failed. Aurora was seen from a ship at about 14.5 N on 1-2 September.
